insight: John tries to count and stops. The end of the story is global, embodied, white-robed worship. The Reformed missionary impulse takes its energy from this scene's certainty.

text: And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death.
insight: Three weapons of the saints' victory — Christ's blood, faithful testimony, willingness to die. Reformed martyrology lives on this verse; the conquest belongs to those who hold these three together.

text: Then I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters and like the sound of mighty peals of thunder, crying out, 'Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.'
insight: The final Hallelujah Chorus in Scripture. Heaven's worship is loud because the reign is real; the Reformed doctrine of God's sovereignty has its hymn here.

text: He who testifies to these things says, 'Surely I am coming soon.' Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!
insight: Scripture closes with a request. The Bible's last word from the saints is a prayer for Christ's return — Maranatha, the Aramaic original of the church's longing.

text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
insight: Bavinck: the imago Dei is the fundamental fact of Christian anthropology — fixed in creation, marred in Eden, restored in Christ. Male and female together carry the image; neither alone exhausts it.

text: And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
insight: The first 'not good' in Scripture is human aloneness. The Reformed doctrine of marriage and friendship begins not with romance but with creation — community is structural, not optional.

text: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel.
insight: The protoevangelium — the first gospel sermon, embedded in the curse. The seed of the woman bruises the serpent's head; Christology begins this early.

text: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing: And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
insight: The Abrahamic covenant in two verses. The promise of blessing 'to all families of the earth' rules out any tribal reading; Paul will name Christ as Abraham's true Seed (Gal 3:16).

text: And he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness.
insight: The verse Paul cites three times to ground justification by faith (Rom 4:3, 9, 22). Abraham is justified by faith before circumcision, before the law — the chronology defends sola fide.

text: And Abraham said, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together.
insight: Abraham's prophecy is wider than he knew. Centuries later, John the Baptist will see Jesus and say 'Behold, the Lamb of God' — the lamb God provided was always Himself.

text: And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest, and will bring thee again into this land; for I will not leave thee, until I have done that which I have spoken to thee of.
insight: Jacob, fleeing his brother, dreams of the ladder. The presence promised here is the presence Jesus claims as his own person in John 1:51 — the ladder is Christ.

text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today.
insight: Joseph's verse of providence. The double 'meant' — same verb, opposite subjects — is the Reformed doctrine of concurrence: human evil and divine good in the same event, both real.

text: God said to Moses, 'I AM WHO I AM.' And he said, 'Say this to the people of Israel: I AM has sent me to you.'
insight: The divine self-naming. YHWH does not derive from anything; he simply is. Reformed theology proper has not progressed beyond the Tetragrammaton, only catechized us into it.

text: And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt.
insight: The blood is the sign for God to see. Passover is the OT typology of substitution: judgment passes by the house where the lamb's blood is, and Christ's blood is the antitype.

text: The Lord is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation: he is my God, and I will prepare him an habitation; my father's God, and I will exalt him.
insight: The Song of Moses after the Red Sea. The Lord becomes 'my' salvation in personal possession; corporate deliverance generates personal worship.

text: And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation. These are the words which thou shalt speak unto the children of Israel.
insight: Israel called to be a kingdom of priests — the corporate vocation Peter applies to the church (1 Peter 2:9). The Reformed doctrine of the priesthood of believers has its OT root here.

text: I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
insight: The first commandment, prefaced by gospel: 'I am the Lord thy God which brought thee out.' Indicative grace before imperative obedience — Reformed catechesis remembers the order.

text: And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest.
insight: Moses bargains with God for the right thing. Not blessing, not victory, but presence — and rest is the surprising consequence. The Reformed pastoral instinct: ask for the Person, not the package.

text: The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,
insight: God's self-revelation to Moses on Sinai — the most-quoted verse about God's character in the OT. Mercy and grace come first; truth and judgment come last. Reformed theology proper memorizes this order.

text: For I am the Lord your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
insight: The 'be holy as I am holy' formula Peter quotes (1 Pet 1:16). Reformed sanctification is participation in God's holiness, not approximation of it; the standard is theocentric.

text: You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the Lord.
insight: Quoted by Jesus as the second great commandment. Long before the Gospels, Israel's law required love of neighbor — and the Reformed read the OT and NT as one moral universe.

text: And I will walk among you, and will be your God, and ye shall be my people.
insight: The covenant formula — I will be your God; you shall be my people. Paul quotes it in 2 Cor 6, and Revelation echoes it at the end (Rev 21:3). The whole Bible can be read as God walking toward this verse's fulfillment.

text: But as truly as I live, all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord.
insight: God's oath to fill the earth with his glory. Whatever rebellion delays, this verse settles — the consummation is not in question. Reformed eschatology rests on the divine self-assertion.

text: God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
insight: Balaam's involuntary prophecy — even pagan oracles cannot resist truth about God. The verse refutes both deistic distance and process-theology drift; God said it, and he will do it.

text: And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the Lord doth man live.
insight: Quoted by Jesus to defeat Satan in the wilderness (Matt 4:4). The wilderness pedagogy — hunger that teaches dependence — is God's classroom for his people then and now.

text: And now, Israel, what doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but to fear the Lord thy God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve the Lord thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul,
insight: What does God require? Five verbs — fear, walk, love, serve, with all your heart. The Reformed catechetical instinct can answer 'what is required' from this verse.

text: The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law.
insight: The Reformed verse on the hidden and revealed will of God. We are responsible for what is revealed; we leave the secret things to him. Every doctrine of providence respects this line.

text: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:
insight: The choice put before Israel: life or death. Reformed monergism does not erase the verse — God's sovereign choice and the creature's responsibility stand together, mysteriously.

text: Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the Lord thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.
insight: Quoted in Hebrews 13:5. 'He will not fail thee, nor forsake thee' is the OT root of NT comfort — and the gospel rests on the same divine reliability.

text: He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.
insight: The Song of Moses' theology proper. Five attributes — Rock, perfect, just, true, righteous — in one verse. Reformed worship still names God this way.

text: The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms: and he shall thrust out the enemy from before thee; and shall say, Destroy them.
insight: The blessing of Moses on the tribes. 'Underneath are the everlasting arms' — Spurgeon preached this verse often; the image of being held by what cannot tire is the Reformed picture of perseverance.

text: And the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:
insight: God's guidance is visible — pillar by day, fire by night. The Reformed instinct: providence is not imperceptible; the means change, the leading does not.

text: And the Lord said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live. And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.
insight: Jesus identifies this as a type of his crucifixion (John 3:14). Looking is the verb of salvation — Reformed soteriology often returns to this image: looking, not laboring.

text: Know therefore that the Lord thy God, he is God, the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him and keep his commandments to a thousand generations;
insight: Three names for the same God — faithful, covenant-keeper, merciful. Reformed covenant theology lives on this verse: God's faithfulness to a thousand generations is not exaggeration but signature.

text: This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.
insight: Meditation 'day and night' echoes Psalm 1. Reformed catechesis insists the leader speaks the law because he meditates on it; mouth and mind run on the same fuel.

text: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
insight: The triple imperative — be strong, of good courage, not afraid — is grounded in 'the Lord thy God is with thee.' Reformed courage is consequential, not self-generated.

text: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.
insight: The household commitment is patriarchal in form, theological in substance. Joshua makes the family the unit of covenant — and the Reformed church has imitated that decision.

text: And the Lord looked upon him, and said, Go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites: have not I sent thee?
insight: Gideon, doubting and small, is sent in his own might because it has been made the Lord's. The Reformed instinct: weakness is a credential when God commissions.

text: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
insight: Ruth's confession is wider than devotion to Naomi — 'thy God shall be my God' is conversion language. Reformed evangelism reads this as a Gentile entering the covenant.

text: The Lord recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
insight: Boaz's blessing prefigures the gospel — refuge under God's wings. Reformed compassion theology echoes here: the Lord rewards the trust of those who shelter under him.

text: There is none holy as the Lord: for there is none beside thee: neither is there any rock like our God.
insight: Hannah's song. 'None holy as the Lord' anchors Reformed worship — God's holiness is unique in kind, not degree.

text: Therefore Eli said unto Samuel, Go, lie down: and it shall be, if he call thee, that thou shalt say, Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth. So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
insight: Eli teaches Samuel to listen. Reformed prayer takes its first verb from this verse — speaking comes second to hearing.

text: And Samuel said, Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
insight: Saul's lesson before his rejection: ritual without obedience is rebellion. The Reformed preference for ordinary obedience over extraordinary sacrifice has its root here.

text: But the Lord said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
insight: Samuel anointing David. The Lord's criteria are not visible to the prophet — and the verse explains every surprising commission since. Reformed pastoral discernment learns to look past appearance.

text: And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build an house for my name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever.
insight: The Davidic covenant — the messianic promise narrows to one house. Reformed Christology runs through this verse to Matthew 1; the Son of David is the kingdom's heir.

text: The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; the God of my rock; in him will I trust: he is my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower, and my refuge, my saviour; thou savest me from violence.
insight: David's deliverance song, parallel to Psalm 18. Seven metaphors for God in two verses — rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn, tower, refuge. Reformed theology proper learns its names here.

text: And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
insight: David refuses to worship cheaply. The verse is the Reformed instinct against cost-free religion — sacrifice that costs nothing is not sacrifice.

text: But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?
insight: Solomon's temple-dedication prayer admits the temple's inadequacy in advance. Reformed worship knows: no space contains God; even the holiest place is condescension.

text: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the Lord be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
insight: Elijah's prosecutorial question — and the people answer with silence. Reformed conviction: the gospel forces decision; eternal hesitation is a vote against.

text: And after the earthquake a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
insight: After the wind and earthquake and fire — the still small voice. Reformed pastoral theology cherishes the verse: God's primary speech is not spectacle but Word.

text: And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.
insight: Elisha to the trembling servant: more with us than with them. The verse is unseen reality reordering the seen — Reformed eschatology in OT form.

text: Turn again, and tell Hezekiah the captain of my people, Thus saith the Lord, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will heal thee: on the third day thou shalt go up unto the house of the Lord.
insight: Hezekiah's deathbed prayer answered before the prophet leaves. The Lord 'hears' and 'sees' — Reformed pastoral theology says prayer is heard in real time, even when answers tarry.

text: Seek the Lord and his strength, seek his face continually.
insight: David's psalm at the ark's installation. The doubled 'seek' — strength and face — is the Reformed posture for the believer: continually after both.

text: If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
insight: The covenant invitation to a divided people. Four verbs of returning — humble, pray, seek, turn — and the promise of healing. Reformed revival theology never tires of this verse.

text: For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.
insight: Ezra's threefold rule for the teacher: to seek, to do, to teach. Reformed exegesis follows this order — study informs life before it informs sermon.

text: O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king's cupbearer.
insight: Nehemiah's intercession before his Persian assignment. The Reformed pastor prays before strategizing — and asks for ears before he asks for outcomes.

text: Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
insight: Ezra reads the law; the people weep; Nehemiah corrects them — joy in the Lord is your strength. Reformed worship learns: confession leads to celebration, not to permanent grief.

text: For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place; but thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed: and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
insight: Mordecai's challenge to Esther. The Reformed reading: providence appoints, but the appointed are still asked to act. Both true; the verse holds them together.

text: Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.
insight: Esther's resolve before approaching the king. The verse models faith that proceeds without guarantees — Reformed courage acts because the King is sovereign, not because the outcome is known.

text: And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
insight: Job's first response to catastrophe. The Reformed read this verse as the gold standard for grief — orthodox, theocentric, blessing-shaped. The Lord gives; the Lord takes; both are praised.

text: But he said unto her, Thou speakest as one of the foolish women speaketh. What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this did not Job sin with his lips.
insight: Job rebukes his wife's counsel of curse-and-die. Reformed theodicy admits that good and evil both come from God's hand, refusing the dualism that would protect God from involvement.

text: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.
insight: The most famous verse of trust under duress. Job will trust even what he cannot understand — the Reformed posture against every fair-weather faith.

text: But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.
insight: Job's confidence in the refining work. The verse refuses to evaluate suffering by its present heat — gold comes out, but only after the fire has done its full work.

text: And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
insight: The wisdom interlude lands here: fear of the Lord is wisdom. After all of Job's debate, the answer is Proverbs 1:7 — and the Reformed catechism agrees.

text: Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind, and said, Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
insight: God's interrogation begins. Reformed theology proper appeals to Job 38-41 against every modern attempt to question God in the dock — the Creator asks the questions.

text: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
insight: Job's first confession from the dust: omnipotence and omniscience together. The Reformed read this as Job catching up to the doctrine Job has always held.

text: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.
insight: Job's repentance after the whirlwind. Hearing becomes seeing; theology becomes encounter. Reformed mysticism (if there is such a thing) lives in this transition.

text: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
insight: The book's thesis. Vanity (hevel) is breath, vapor, mist — not 'worthless' but 'wisp-like.' The Preacher's whole project is teaching how to live in fog without losing the way.

text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
insight: The famous verse on seasons. Reformed providence reads this not as fatalism but as ordered time — God assigns the moments, and the believer learns to recognize each.

text: For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.
insight: The Preacher's anthropology. Total depravity proven in two lines — there is none who does good without sinning. Romans 3 will quote a similar conclusion.

text: Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
insight: The Preacher's pastoral counsel to the young. The Reformed catechism includes this verse: youth should remember the Creator before the years rebel.

text: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.
insight: The shepherd's love-banner over the beloved. Read mystically by the Puritans (Owen, Sibbes) as Christ's covenanted affection for the soul.

text: I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies.
insight: The mutual possession formula. Reformed expositors (Spurgeon especially) hear this as the believer's confession of union with Christ — owned and owning.

text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
insight: God's invitation to negotiate forgiveness. The colour transformation — scarlet to snow — is the chemistry of justification: dyed-in cleansed-out. Reformed proclamation borrows this verse for evangelistic invitation.

text: Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
insight: The Immanuel sign Matthew quotes for the virgin birth (Matt 1:23). The name itself — God with us — is the gospel in noun form.

text: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
insight: Isaiah's confidence in the day of salvation. The triple — salvation, strength, song — names the believer's daily posture. Reformed worship sings because the Lord has become both verb and noun of rescue.

text: For thus saith the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
insight: Four nouns of salvation — returning, rest, quietness, confidence — that Israel refused. Reformed pastoral counsel hears every age of the church refusing these same gifts.

text: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
insight: The verse on the durability of God's word. Reformed homiletics finds in this verse permission to preach with confidence — what is fading is not what is being preached.

text: All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.
insight: The atonement verse Reformed theology returns to. The 'all' of human sin meets the 'him' of divine substitution; the burden has been transferred.

text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
insight: The gospel call extends to those who can pay nothing. Reformed proclamation reads this verse as the universal offer — without money and without price.

text: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
insight: The word's productivity. Reformed preaching trusts this verse — what is sown will accomplish what God sent it for, regardless of immediate evidence.

text: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound;
insight: Jesus reads this passage in Nazareth (Luke 4:18). The Spirit-anointing mission has its OT scripture; Reformed missiology cites both verses together.

text: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.
insight: God's election precedes the womb. Reformed soteriology cites this verse not only for vocational calling but for the priority of grace in every life.

text: Thus saith the Lord, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the Lord which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth.
insight: The three glories denied — wisdom, might, riches — and the one glory permitted: understanding the Lord. Reformed theology's first principle is recognizable here.

text: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the Lord. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.
insight: The potter and clay image. Romans 9 will repurpose this — Paul's strongest defense of sovereignty has its OT root here.

text: Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the Lord. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord.
insight: Omnipresence stated as God's own question. Reformed theology proper hears this verse against every account of God's limitation; nowhere is unobserved.

text: But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the Lord, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
insight: The new covenant promise — law internalized, not merely posted. Hebrews 8 will quote this as the Christian covenant's character; the Spirit's work has its prophetic charter here.

text: Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not.
insight: God's invitation to inquire. Reformed prayer is bold because the Inviter has issued the call — 'great and mighty things' are offered to those who ask.

text: The Lord is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him.
insight: Lamentations' refrain on waiting. After the destruction of Jerusalem, the verse insists the Lord is good to those who wait — a Reformed pastoral comfort in the worst weeks.

text: But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men.
insight: God grieves; God shows compassion. The verse insists divine sorrow over judgment is real — Reformed theology refuses to flatten the divine pathos.

text: Turn thou us unto thee, O Lord, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old.
insight: The Lamentation prayer for restoration. Reformed monergism reads it directly — only God can turn the hearts he has scattered; the verse is the asking.

text: Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord God, and thou becamest mine.
insight: Covenant as marriage. Reformed federal theology reads this verse as God's nuptial commitment — the OT covenants prefigure the Bridegroom Lamb of Revelation.

text: Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord God: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?
insight: God's stated reluctance toward judgment. Reformed exegesis takes seriously the divine 'no pleasure' in wickedness — judgment is just but not preferred.

text: And I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.
insight: The Spirit's promised work in the new covenant. Reformed sanctification reads obedience as Spirit-enabled walking, not just morality coached from outside.

text: Thus saith the Lord God unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live:
insight: The dry bones vision's central verse. Reformed soteriology — only the Spirit's breath makes the dead live — has its picture here. Regeneration is resurrection language.

text: And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
insight: Daniel's response to mystery revealed: God reigns over times and kingdoms. Reformed political theology never tires of this verse — empires are subordinate, not ultimate.

text: And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?
insight: Nebuchadnezzar's restored confession. The Reformed doctrine of God's sole rule has this verse — and the pagan king becomes its mouthpiece.

text: I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
insight: Daniel's vision of the Son of Man — Jesus's favorite self-designation. Reformed Christology runs from this verse through the Gospels to Hebrews.

text: And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
insight: The promise to the wise — they shall shine like stars. Reformed eschatology honors the verse: humble faithfulness will be conspicuous in the age to come.

text: And I will sow her unto me in the earth; and I will have mercy upon her that had not obtained mercy; and I will say to them which were not my people, Thou art my people; and they shall say, Thou art my God.
insight: The covenant reversal: not-my-people becomes my-people. Peter and Paul both quote this verse (Rom 9:25, 1 Pet 2:10) to ground Gentile inclusion. Reformed federal theology hears Gentile incorporation foreseen.

text: Take with you words, and turn to the Lord: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips.
insight: Hosea's altar call. 'Take with you words' is the verse for those who can offer nothing else — repentance has no requirement but bringing the words God has given.

text: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
insight: The Lord restores what locusts have eaten — Reformed pastoral theology cherishes this as the verse for those whose decades feel devoured. Restoration is in God's vocabulary.

text: And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions:
insight: The Pentecost prophecy Peter quotes (Acts 2:17). The Spirit's outpouring on 'all flesh' is the OT root of the Reformed catholic vision: barriers of gender, age, status fall before the Spirit.

text: And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered: for in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance, as the Lord hath said, and in the remnant whom the Lord shall call.
insight: The verse Paul cites in Romans 10:13 — 'whosoever shall call.' The universal offer of salvation has its OT charter; the gospel name to invoke is the Lord's.

text: Therefore thus will I do unto thee, O Israel: and because I will do this unto thee, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.
insight: The repeated 'yet have ye not returned' (4:6-11) lands here. The verse the Reformed conscience hears in every season of unrepented sin — prepare to meet the One who summons.

text: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord God, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord:
insight: The worst famine — not bread, but the word. Reformed homiletics reads this verse as a warning to a Western church that has plenty of books and few hearings.

text: Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
insight: God reveals his counsel to his prophets. Reformed doctrine of revelation hears here both the priority of God's initiative and the role of human messengers.

text: And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the Lord's.
insight: The kingdom shall be the Lord's. Reformed eschatology cites this verse — the smallest book in the OT closes with the largest claim.

text: And he said unto them, I am an Hebrew; and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land.
insight: Jonah's witness in transit. Even the fleeing prophet confesses the right doctrine — and the sailors believe before he repents. The verse mocks the messenger and honors the message.

text: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?
insight: The book's last verse — a question, not a resolution. God's mercy reaches even ignorance and animals; Jonah is left to decide whether he can stomach a wider God.

text: But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
insight: The Bethlehem prophecy. Matthew 2 will quote it; the Magi will follow it. The Reformed read this as proof of providential precision — even the village is foretold.

text: Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.
insight: Micah's astonishment at God's pardoning. The verse is the Reformed doxology of forgiveness — there is no God like ours, and the proof is mercy.

text: The Lord is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the Lord hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
insight: Two attributes balanced — slow to anger, great in power. Reformed theology proper refuses to let either eclipse the other; the patience and the wrath are both real.

text: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
insight: The verse Paul quotes three times (Rom 1:17, Gal 3:11, Heb 10:38). 'The just shall live by his faith' — the Reformation's text in its original setting.

text: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
insight: The promise that knowledge of God's glory will saturate the earth as the waters cover the sea. Reformed missiology rests on this verse — the consummation is universal recognition.

text: The great day of the Lord is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly, even the voice of the day of the Lord: the mighty man shall cry there bitterly.
insight: The day of the Lord — near and hastening. Reformed eschatology takes seriously both the imminence and the inevitability; the verse refuses to let the church be casual about it.

text: For then will I turn to the people a pure language, that they may all call upon the name of the Lord, to serve him with one consent.
insight: The reversal of Babel — pure language given to all peoples. Reformed missiology reads this verse as gospel undoing Genesis 11; the Lord re-unifies what sin scattered.

text: Now therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts; Consider your ways.
insight: Haggai's refrain after seventy years of distracted building. 'Consider your ways' — the Reformed examination of conscience has this verse as its prompt.

text: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
insight: Palm Sunday's prophecy. Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey to fulfill this verse precisely — Reformed Christology never tires of pointing out the literal correspondence.

text: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.
insight: The pierced One looked upon. John 19:37 cites this verse at the crucifixion. Reformed Christology reads it as Trinitarian — they pierced me (YHWH speaking), and he is the One pierced.

text: For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the Lord of hosts.
insight: From sunrise to sunset, the Lord's name shall be great among the nations. Reformed missiology cites this verse — even before the New Covenant, the geographical scope was global.

text: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
insight: The Lord's invitation to test him in tithing. Reformed stewardship reads this verse — generous return is the believer's reasoned response to a giving God.

text: But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
insight: The Sun of righteousness rising with healing in his wings — the last messianic prophecy of the OT. Reformed Christology hears Christ's coming announced in solar terms.

text: Love, and do what you will. If you keep silence, keep silence with love; if you cry out, cry out with love; if you correct, correct with love; if you spare, spare with love. Let the root of love be within you, and from that root nothing but good can spring.
ref: Homilies on the First Epistle of John, VII.8
insight: Often shortened to 'love and do what you will' and misused as license. Augustine's full sentence makes love a root that disciplines its own branches — the freedom is grounded in the rule of love, not its absence.

text: I heard a voice from the neighbouring house, as of a boy or girl, I know not which, chanting and oft repeating, 'Take up and read; take up and read.' I rose, interpreting it to be no other than a command from God to open the book and read the first chapter I should find.
insight: The Tolle, lege conversion. Augustine opens Romans, reads 13:13-14, and the long resistance breaks. The Reformed know this pattern — Scripture reaches the heart that has been long under conviction.

text: If you understand, it is not God.
insight: Augustine's principle of theological humility — comprehension would make God a creature. Reformed theology takes the apophatic side of doctrine seriously here; God exceeds what minds can contain.

text: I desire to know God and the soul. Nothing more? Nothing whatever.
insight: Augustine's intellectual program in a single exchange. The early Reformed catechists adopted this as their own discipline — knowing God deeply, knowing oneself honestly, both at once.

text: Two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
insight: The hinge of City of God. Augustine reads history through two loves — and the Reformed instinct against worldly accommodation hears here the original analysis.

text: He was not, as might be imagined, circumscribed in the body; nor, while He was in the body, was He absent from elsewhere... He was at once everywhere.
insight: Athanasius on what later Reformed theologians called the extra Calvinisticum: the Word fills the universe even while incarnate. Reformed Christology has read this passage with delight.

text: It was unfitting that creatures made by God should be brought to nothing through the deceit wrought upon man by the devil; and supremely unfitting that the work of God in mankind should disappear.
insight: Athanasius gives the metaphysical reason for the incarnation: God's goodness will not let his work perish. Reformed soteriology hears in this the priority of divine love over creaturely failure.

text: These are the springs of salvation, that he who thirsts may be satisfied with the living words they contain. In these alone the doctrine of godliness is proclaimed. Let no one add to these; let no one take away from them.
insight: The earliest catalogue of the 27 New Testament books — Athanasius lists what the church will recognize as canon. Reformed bibliology cites his Festal Letter for the canon's reception.

text: It was necessary for man's salvation that there should be a knowledge revealed by God besides philosophical science... For man is directed to God as to an end that surpasses the grasp of his reason.
insight: The opening question of the Summa: why revealed theology is needed in addition to natural reason. The Reformed instinct against rationalist sufficiency hears Aquinas here, even as the traditions differ on natural theology's reach.

text: Charity is the love by which God is loved for his own sake, and our neighbor for God's sake.
insight: Aquinas defines charity strictly: not love for what God gives, but love for who God is — and neighbor-love grounded in the same. Reformed devotion has not improved on this distinction; the affection terminates on the Person.

text: I devoutly adore you, hidden Deity, truly hidden beneath these appearances. My whole heart submits to you, for in contemplating you, it surrenders itself completely.
insight: The Eucharistic hymn Aquinas wrote in 1264. Reformed readers can affirm the adoration of the hidden Christ even as they differ on the elements' theology — the longing to behold him is shared.

text: The final happiness of man consists in the contemplation of God by the intellect, with the love of God moving the will.
insight: Aquinas's account of human flourishing terminates in knowing and loving God. The Reformed catechism translates the same instinct: chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him forever.

text: The will of man stands as a beast of burden between two riders. If God mounts it, it wills and goes whither God wills; if Satan mounts it, it wills and goes whither Satan wills. Nor can it choose to which rider it will run, but the riders themselves contend which shall have and hold it.
insight: Luther's metaphor for the bondage of the will against Erasmus. Reformed monergism cites this passage to anchor the necessity of divine initiative — neither rider chooses the mount.

text: A theologian of glory calls evil good and good evil. A theologian of the cross calls the thing what it actually is.
insight: Luther's theology of the cross against medieval glory-theology. Reformed preaching learns from this thesis to start where God starts — at the cross, not at the spectacular.

text: Of this article one cannot yield or surrender any part... On this article rests all that we teach and practice against the pope, the devil, and the world.
insight: Luther's resolve on justification by faith. Reformed confessionalism agrees — there is no negotiable doctrine if this one falls.

text: I would not give up Christ for all the world or even for the whole Catholic church on earth. He has done so much for me that I can never deny him.
insight: Luther's pastoral counsel: do not surrender Christ for any institution. Reformed loyalty has always been to Christ first, the visible church second — even when the visible church is contested.

text: A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none. A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.
ref: The Freedom of a Christian (1520), opening theses
insight: Luther's paradox of Christian freedom. Reformed sanctification holds both poles — free from condemnation, bound to serve in love, simultaneously and without contradiction.

text: Did we in our own strength confide, our striving would be losing; were not the right Man on our side, the Man of God's own choosing. Dost ask who that may be? Christ Jesus, it is he.
ref: Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott (1529)
insight: Luther's hymn translates Psalm 46 into Reformation theology. The 'right Man' is Christ, chosen by God for the battle — Reformed worship still sings what Luther wrote.

text: When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, 'Repent,' he willed that the whole life of believers should be one of repentance.
insight: Luther's first thesis frames the Christian life as continuous return. Reformed sanctification reads the verb as habitual, not episodic — repentance is a posture, not a punctuated event.

text: Faith is a firm and certain knowledge of God's benevolence toward us, founded upon the truth of the freely given promise in Christ, both revealed to our minds and sealed upon our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
insight: Calvin's definition of faith in three motions: knowledge (firm), promise (in Christ), Spirit (sealing). Reformed catechism has not improved on this triple structure.

text: Prayer is an intercourse of men with God, by which, having entered the heavenly sanctuary, they appeal to him in person concerning his promises.
insight: Calvin reads prayer as conversation — intercourse, not transaction. Reformed prayer theology owes this passage the relational frame.

text: Let us learn from her single title of mother how useful, indeed how necessary, the knowledge of her is, since there is no other means of entering into life unless she conceive us in her womb, give us birth, nourish us at her breast.
insight: Calvin's strong ecclesiology, quoting Cyprian. Reformed federal theology takes seriously the church's instrumental role: salvation is personal, not solitary.

text: The same Spirit who has spoken through the mouths of the prophets must penetrate into our hearts to persuade us that they faithfully proclaimed what had been divinely commanded.
insight: Calvin's internal testimony of the Spirit (testimonium internum Spiritus Sancti). Reformed bibliology rests its assurance of Scripture not on argument alone but on the Spirit's persuasion.

text: Justification is the principal hinge by which religion is supported.
insight: Calvin names justification as the hinge of religion (cardinem religionis). Reformed Protestantism never tires of saying it — Luther agreed nine years before Calvin's Institutes.

text: There is no people so barbarous, no nation so brutal, as not to be imbued with the conviction that there is a God.
insight: Calvin's sensus divinitatis — the seed of religion sown in every person. Reformed apologetics rests on this universal sense; atheism is a position requiring effort.

text: Set faith at work on Christ for the killing of thy sin. His blood is the great sovereign remedy for sin-sick souls.
insight: Owen's pastoral counsel in the trenches of sin. Reformed sanctification has its method here: faith applied to Christ specifically for mortification, not in general for forgiveness only.

text: Beholding the glory of Christ by faith is the only way to grow in grace and likeness to him.
insight: Owen's late work on contemplative Christology. Reformed sanctification follows 2 Cor 3:18 — transformation by beholding, not by trying.

text: The end of Christ's death was not to make our salvation possible, but to make it certain. The Father gave him a people, the Son redeemed that people, the Spirit applies that redemption — and none of the three persons fail in their work.
ref: The Death of Death in the Death of Christ (1647), Book I
insight: Owen's argument for definite atonement — and against any account that detaches the cross from its purchased outcomes. Reformed atonement (definite, particular, effectual) found in Owen its most rigorous defender.

text: To be carnally minded is death; to be spiritually minded is life and peace. There is a frame of mind, a complexion of soul, which God allows and approves; and there is another which he disallows and condemns.
insight: Owen's exposition of Romans 8:6. Reformed pastoral theology learned from Owen to read the inward life carefully — the frame of mind is itself a moral state.

text: Indwelling sin always abides while we are in this world; therefore it is always to be mortified.
insight: Owen's premise: sin's residence is permanent; mortification's labor must be too. Reformed sanctification is not eradication but constant warfare — and Romans 8:13 grounds the campaign.

text: There is nothing in religion that any man hath, who hath not received it; nor doth any man receive anything but what is given him from above.
insight: Owen's monergistic anthropology of grace. Reformed theology of regeneration finds no room for the autonomous self-starter — what is had has been given, top to bottom.

text: Believers are to consider what Christ's love is, that they may not measure it by their own thoughts of themselves.
insight: Owen's counsel against measuring Christ's love by our self-judgment. Reformed assurance leans on this: Christ's love is fixed by what it is, not by what we feel about it.

text: It appears that all that is ever spoken of in the Scripture as an ultimate end of God's works, is included in that one phrase, 'the glory of God.'
ref: The End for Which God Created the World (1765)
insight: Edwards's account of God's purpose in creation: glory radiating outward. Reformed teleology has not improved on this — God's chief end and ours overlap (cf. WSC Q.1).

text: The affections are no other than the more vigorous and sensible exercises of the inclination and will of the soul.
insight: Edwards on affections — not feelings in the sentimental sense, but vigorous motions of the will. Reformed psychology treats the affections seriously because Edwards taught us to.

text: Christian practice or a holy life is a great and distinguishing sign of true and saving grace.
insight: Edwards on the most important sign of true conversion: holy practice. Reformed examination of conscience reads with Edwards — feelings can deceive; sustained obedience is harder to fake.

text: The wrath of God burns against them, their damnation does not slumber; the pit is prepared, the fire is made ready, the furnace is now hot, ready to receive them.
ref: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God (1741)
insight: Edwards's most-known sermon — preached calmly to a Northampton congregation that began to weep. Reformed preaching of judgment owes its seriousness to sermons that took hell seriously without theatricality.

text: The first instance that I remember of that sort of inward, sweet delight in God and divine things... was on reading those words, 1 Tim. 1:17. As I read the words, there came into my soul, and was as it were diffused through it, a sense of the glory of the Divine Being.
insight: Edwards records his own conversion-experience triggered by a single text. Reformed pastoral theology reads conversion narratives because the Word's work is always personal.

text: Love is the sum of all that is good — the fountain of every other holy disposition — the source of all that is in heaven.
ref: Charity and Its Fruits (1738), Lecture I
insight: Edwards on heaven's economy. Reformed eschatology, refined through Edwards's sermon series, treats heaven as the consummation of love — not the absence of activity but its purification.

text: There is in Christ Jesus an admirable conjunction of diverse excellencies. There do meet in Jesus Christ infinite highness and infinite condescension; infinite justice and infinite grace; infinite glory and lowest humility.
insight: Edwards's sermon on Revelation 5:5-6. Reformed Christology stretches between attributes that seem opposite — Edwards taught the church to see them as harmony, not paradox.

text: The Calvinist is the man who sees God. He has caught sight of the ineffable Vision, and he will not let it fade for a moment from his eyes.
insight: Warfield's compact summary of the Reformed instinct. To see God truly is to see oneself rightly — and the Calvinist's preoccupation with God's sovereignty flows from that prior seeing.

text: Calvinism is just religion in its purity. We have only, therefore, to conceive of religion in its purest form to conceive of it as Calvinism.
insight: Warfield's polemic claim. Reformed self-understanding has often borrowed his framing — Calvinism not as a faction but as religion stripped to its essentials.

text: Inspiration is a supernatural influence exerted on the sacred writers by the Spirit of God, by virtue of which their writings are given divine trustworthiness.
insight: Warfield's classic definition. Reformed bibliology rests on this account: inspiration is what makes the writings what they are, not what they become through the church's use.

text: Christianity may be defined, in a word, as the religion of salvation by grace.
insight: Warfield's compressed gospel. Reformed soteriology agrees — grace is not one feature among many but the genus under which the whole Christian religion is classified.

text: There is no aspect of human life which is not, in some sense, governed by the saving work of Christ.
ref: Selected Shorter Writings, vol. 1 (paraphrasing his argument)
insight: Warfield's account of Christ's cosmic relevance. Reformed worldview pushes this conviction outward — there is no neutral zone where the gospel does not have purchase.

text: There is no holiness in this life apart from progressive sanctification, with conflict and growth held together.
ref: Perfectionism (1931 posth.), vol. I (summary of argument)
insight: Warfield's two-volume rebuttal of Holiness-movement perfectionism. Reformed sanctification accepts both conflict and growth — the believer is being made holy, but is not yet sinless.

text: To unfold the Apostle's eschatology means to set forth his theology as a whole.
insight: Vos's thesis on Paul: eschatology is not one locus among many but the structural frame of Pauline thought. Reformed biblical theology took this insight and rebuilt its curriculum.

text: Biblical theology deals with the revelation of God in its historical progress.
ref: Biblical Theology: Old and New Testaments (1948), ch. 1
insight: Vos defined biblical theology as history-of-revelation. Reformed seminaries owe him the discipline — Scripture's content is held together by its unfolding storyline, not just by systematic loci.

text: Faith deals with eternity in time. It is the soul's quiet appropriation of what God has already accomplished in Christ.
insight: Vos in the pulpit — biblical theology pastoral. Faith does not bring eternity nearer; it recognizes that eternity has already arrived in Christ.

text: The kingdom of God, in our Lord's teaching, is both present and future; both an inward state and an outward order.
ref: The Teaching of Jesus Concerning the Kingdom and the Church (1903), ch. 2
insight: Vos articulates the already / not-yet decades before the term became fashionable. Reformed eschatology learned to hold both tenses because Vos taught the church to read the Gospels with both.

text: The resurrection of Christ is the central act of the new age breaking in upon the old.
insight: Vos's reading of resurrection as eschatology realized. Reformed soteriology of union with Christ owes Vos this framing — believers are already in the age Christ inaugurated.

text: Dogmatics is the system of the knowledge of God, the knowledge which he himself has given us in his revelation.
insight: Bavinck's opening definition. Reformed dogmatics is not natural philosophy but exposition of given revelation — and the order is God's, not the systematician's.

text: In the doctrine of the Trinity beats the heart of the whole revelation of God.
insight: Bavinck reads the Trinity not as one doctrine among many but as the doctrine that gives all others their pulse. Reformed worship learned from Bavinck to treat the triunity as definitional, not decorative.

text: The whole of Christ's person and work is the heart of the gospel; the incarnation and the cross are not two messages but one.
ref: Reformed Dogmatics, III (Sin and Salvation in Christ)
insight: Bavinck refuses to isolate the cross from the rest of the gospel narrative. Reformed Christology with Bavinck reads incarnation through resurrection as a single saving event with three acts.

text: The Christian religion is, by its very nature, catholic. It is meant for every age, every race, and every culture.
ref: Reformed Dogmatics, IV (Holy Spirit, Church, and New Creation)
insight: Bavinck's defense of the church's universal scope against parochial tendencies. Reformed catholicity (small-c) reads the Reformation as continuity with the apostolic church, not a new founding.

text: Doctrine produces worldview by inner necessity; the doctrine of God leads, of itself, to a Christian way of seeing everything.
insight: Bavinck's organic theology: doctrine produces worldview, not the other way around. The Reformed worldview tradition (Kuyper, then American neo-Calvinism) has its root in this conviction.

text: The plain fact is that liberalism, whether it be true or false, is no mere 'heresy' — no mere divergence at isolated points from Christian teaching. On the contrary, it proceeds from a totally different root, and it constitutes, in essentials, a unitary system of its own.
insight: Machen's diagnostic distinction. Reformed confessionalism after Machen has refused to treat liberalism as a wayward Christianity — the disagreement is at the root, not the branches.

text: Faith is, then, the recognition of a fact — the fact of the loving will of God and the saving work of Christ.
insight: Machen against fideism and against rationalist Christianity. Faith is response to fact — Reformed catechesis can teach faith without making it irrational or making it credentialless.

text: Christianity began as a message that something had happened. It was, at its inception, a way of life founded upon news.
insight: Machen's historical anchor. The Christian movement is not advice but news — and Reformed proclamation has not moved past this distinction.

text: Paul's religion is rooted in Jesus, and yet it is a religion that asserts Jesus to be the Christ, the Son of God.
ref: The Origin of Paul's Religion (1921), ch. 1
insight: Machen against the History-of-Religions school that wanted to separate Paul from Jesus. Reformed Pauline theology agrees: the disciple did not invent the Master's identity; the Master claimed it first.

text: Faith must take account of the contents of Scripture, not merely of personal experience.
ref: The Christian Faith in the Modern World (1936)
insight: Machen's discipline against subjectivist drift. Reformed catechesis follows: Scripture supplies the doctrines that experience may then warm — the order matters.

text: A man who was merely a man and said the sort of things Jesus said would not be a great moral teacher. He would either be a lunatic — on a level with the man who says he is a poached egg — or else he would be the Devil of Hell.
insight: Lewis's famous Liar-Lunatic-Lord trilemma. Reformed apologetics has noted the limits of the argument while honoring its force — the verse forces a verdict that 'great moral teacher' was never on the table.

text: To love at all is to be vulnerable. Love anything, and your heart will certainly be wrung and possibly be broken. If you want to make sure of keeping it intact, you must give your heart to no one, not even to an animal.
insight: Lewis on love's necessary risk. Reformed pastoral counsel honors this paragraph: there is no safe love, and the closed heart is not preserved but ossified.

text: I gave in, and admitted that God was God, and knelt and prayed: perhaps, that night, the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England.
insight: Lewis's reluctant conversion. Reformed pastoral theology honors this narrative — the will resists, the heart yields, and the moment of surrender often feels nothing like victory.

text: In commanding us to glorify Him, God is inviting us to enjoy Him.
insight: Lewis untying the doxology / hedonism knot. Reformed catechesis (WSC Q.1) has read this line ever since — glory and joy are not parallel goals but one motion.

text: What is preaching? Logic on fire! Eloquent reason! Are these contradictions? Of course they are not. Preaching is theology coming through a man who is on fire.
insight: Lloyd-Jones's most-quoted definition. Reformed homiletics holds together the two halves — without the logic, fire is sentiment; without the fire, logic is lecture.

text: The Beatitudes are not natural to anyone. They cut across every natural inclination of the human heart.
ref: Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, vol. 1
insight: Lloyd-Jones on the Sermon's grain. Reformed soteriology agrees: the Beatitudes describe regenerated dispositions, not common decency improved.

text: The Christian is something entirely new — something that the world has never seen before; something so different that the world cannot understand it.
ref: Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, vol. 2 (Salt and Light)
insight: Lloyd-Jones on identity. Reformed sanctification reads this verse against every accommodationist drift — the Christian is constituted by what the world cannot produce.

text: There is no more central, no more vital theme in all the Bible than the cross of Christ.
insight: Lloyd-Jones's last book on the verse all his others led to. Reformed proclamation follows: the cross is not one chapter of the gospel but the chapter through which all others are read.

text: The whole purpose of the gospel is to bring people to know God.
insight: Lloyd-Jones on the telos. Reformed soteriology terminates in knowing — not just having sins forgiven, but coming into communion with the Person who forgives.

text: Christianity means community through Jesus Christ and in Jesus Christ. No Christian community is more or less than this.
insight: Bonhoeffer's opening definition. Reformed ecclesiology agrees: the church is not a club around Christ but a community in him — the preposition matters.

text: He who loves his dream of a community more than the community itself becomes a destroyer of the latter, even though his personal intentions may be ever so honest, earnest, and sacrificial.
insight: Bonhoeffer against community-as-projection. Reformed pastoral theology reads this as a warning to every idealist who loves the church he imagines more than the church he has.

text: Cheap grace is grace without discipleship, grace without the cross, grace without Jesus Christ, living and incarnate.
insight: Bonhoeffer's negative definition that defines the positive. Reformed grace is costly because it cost the Son's life — and refusing the cost cheapens the gift.

text: Costly grace is the kingly rule of God, for which a man will gladly go and sell all that he has. It is the pearl of great price to buy which the merchant will sell all his goods.
insight: Bonhoeffer's positive picture. The Reformed read this not as works-salvation but as gospel-shaped joy: what costs everything is what we gladly pay for, because what we get is worth more.

text: Only the suffering God can help.
ref: Letters and Papers from Prison (1944), letter of 16 July
insight: Bonhoeffer from prison. Reformed Christology reads this not as theopaschism but as incarnation taken to its end — the God who came near in flesh suffered, and that nearness is the help.

text: Who stands fast? Only the man whose final standard is not his reason, his principles, his conscience, his freedom, or his virtue, but who is ready to sacrifice all this when he is called to obedient and responsible action in faith.
ref: Letters and Papers from Prison, 'After Ten Years' (Christmas 1942)
insight: Bonhoeffer's diagnostic question for a totalitarian age. Reformed ethics reads this as the demand that faith outrank every penultimate virtue — including conscience itself, when conscience is conscripted by ideology.

text: It is only by living completely in this world that one learns to have faith.
ref: Letters and Papers from Prison, 21 July 1944
insight: Bonhoeffer against monastic escape. Reformed worldview thinking honors this — faith is forged in vocational presence to the actual world, not in retreat from it.

text: Christ took upon himself this world's guilt to its uttermost depth, and there is no longer any human guilt that has not been laid on him.
insight: Bonhoeffer on the breadth of atonement's reach. Reformed atonement theology hears here the verse from 1 John 1:9 in dogmatic statement — no sin lies outside the assumed weight.

text: Disregard the study of God, and you sentence yourself to stumble and blunder through life blindfold, as it were, with no sense of direction and no understanding of what surrounds you.
insight: Packer's pastoral case for doctrine. Reformed catechesis treats knowing God as life-orientation, not as a graduate seminar — without it, the rest of life is unmapped.

text: God's wisdom is not, and never was, pledged to keep a fallen world happy, or to make ungodliness comfortable.
ref: Knowing God (1973), ch. 9 ('God's Wisdom and Ours')
insight: Packer against pious mismeasurement. Reformed providence reads this verse against every reading of God's wisdom that turns it into a comfort-engineering plan.

text: Adoption is the highest privilege that the gospel offers: higher even than justification.
insight: Packer's ranking surprised many evangelicals. Reformed soteriology with Packer reads adoption as the gospel's apex — justification declares status; adoption gives the Father.

text: The doctrine of justification by faith is like Atlas: it bears a world on its shoulders, the entire evangelical knowledge of saving grace.
ref: Knowing God (1973), ch. 18 ('The Heart of the Gospel')
insight: Packer's structural metaphor. Reformed Protestantism agrees — every other gospel doctrine sits on justification, and the rest collapses when this one moves.

text: God sets his love upon men — God, the great I AM, the God who is to be feared, fixes his love on you.
ref: Knowing God (1973), ch. 12 ('The Love of God')
insight: Packer on the wonder of being chosen. Reformed assurance has its source: the God great enough to terrify is the same God who fixes love on his people by name.

text: Holiness, for the Puritans, was not solemnity but joy — the joy of beholding and reflecting the beauty of God.
insight: Packer's corrective to the dour Puritan caricature. Reformed sanctification reads the Puritans as joyful seekers of God's beauty, not as moralists with grim faces.

text: The gospel is news, good news — that God has done something for our salvation that we could never do for ourselves.
insight: Packer's catechetical compression. Reformed proclamation can be taught from this sentence — gospel is announcement of accomplished work, not advice on attainable virtue.

text: There is, we must remind ourselves, a difference between knowing about God and knowing God.
insight: Packer's diagnostic distinction. Reformed catechesis insists on both — information that does not become acquaintance has stopped short of the verse's promise (John 17:3).
